Title: What Is GraphQL vs REST in 1 Page
Desc: A simple comparison of GraphQL and REST APIs, including how they work, their advantages, disadvantages, and when developers should choose one over the other.
Author: Core Lord
Data:
## If you've built web applications, you've probably encountered two common ways to fetch data:

```text
REST
```

and

```text id="graphql-name"
GraphQL
```

Both solve the same problem:

```text id="api-goal"
Client
↓
Request Data
↓
Server
↓
Return Data
```

But they approach that problem differently.

This guide explains GraphQL and REST in simple terms and helps you understand when each makes sense.

---

## What Is REST?

REST (Representational State Transfer) is the traditional way many web APIs work.

Resources are exposed through URLs.

Example:

```http id="rest-user"
GET /users/1
```

Response:

```json id="rest-response"
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "John"
}
```

Different resources typically have different endpoints.

Examples:

```http id="rest-endpoints"
GET /users
GET /posts
GET /comments
```

REST has been the dominant API style for many years.

---

## What Is GraphQL?

GraphQL is a query language for APIs.

Instead of requesting data from multiple endpoints, clients ask for exactly what they need.

Example:

```graphql id="graphql-query"
{
  user(id: 1) {
    name
    email
  }
}
```

Response:

```json id="graphql-response"
{
  "data": {
    "user": {
      "name": "John",
      "email": "john@example.com"
    }
  }
}
```

The client defines the shape of the response.

---

![Developer working with API requests and responses](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1571171637578-41bc2dd41cd2)

# REST vs GraphQL: The Core Difference

REST:

```text id="rest-flow"
Server Defines Response
```

GraphQL:

```text id="graphql-flow"
Client Defines Response
```

This difference affects how applications fetch and manage data.

---

## REST Example

Suppose you're building a profile page.

You need:

* User name
* User email
* User posts

REST requests might look like:

```http id="rest-user-api"
GET /users/1
```

and:

```http id="rest-post-api"
GET /users/1/posts
```

Multiple requests may be required.

---

## GraphQL Example

The same information can often be requested with a single query:

```graphql id="graphql-profile"
{
  user(id: 1) {
    name
    email
    posts {
      title
    }
  }
}
```

One request.

One response.

---

## Understanding Over-Fetching

REST APIs sometimes return more data than needed.

Example:

```json id="over-fetch"
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "John",
  "email": "john@example.com",
  "phone": "...",
  "address": "...",
  "preferences": "..."
}
```

But the page only needs:

```text id="needed"
Name
Email
```

Extra data is downloaded unnecessarily.

This is called:

```text id="overfetch-name"
Over-Fetching
```

---

## Understanding Under-Fetching

Sometimes REST provides too little data.

Example:

```text id="under-fetch"
User Data
↓
Need Posts
↓
Need Comments
↓
Need Additional Requests
```

Multiple requests become necessary.

This is called:

```text id="underfetch-name"
Under-Fetching
```

GraphQL was partly designed to address both issues.

# Advantages of REST

REST remains extremely popular for good reasons.

---

## Simple to Understand

REST follows straightforward patterns:

```text id="rest-pattern"
GET
POST
PUT
DELETE
```

Developers learn it quickly.

---

## Excellent Tooling

REST is supported by:

* Browsers
* Frameworks
* Hosting providers
* Documentation tools

Almost every platform understands REST.

---

## Easy Caching

HTTP caching works naturally with REST endpoints.

Example:

```http id="cache-example"
GET /products
```

Browsers and CDNs can cache responses efficiently.

---

## Mature Ecosystem

REST has existed for decades.

Documentation, tutorials, and tools are abundant.

---

# Advantages of GraphQL

GraphQL provides several unique benefits.

---

## Request Exactly What You Need

Example:

```graphql id="exact-query"
{
  user {
    name
  }
}
```

Only the requested fields are returned.

---

## Fewer Requests

Complex data can often be fetched in a single query.

This is particularly useful for mobile applications.

---

## Strongly Typed Schema

GraphQL APIs define available fields and relationships.

Developers can explore APIs more easily.

---

## Better Developer Experience

Many GraphQL tools provide:

* Auto-completion
* Query validation
* Schema exploration

These features improve productivity.

---

![Frontend and backend integration using APIs](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1555066931-4365d14bab8c)

# Disadvantages of REST

REST isn't perfect.

Common challenges include:

### Over-Fetching

Too much data returned.

---

### Under-Fetching

Too many requests required.

---

### Endpoint Growth

Large systems may accumulate:

```text id="many-endpoints"
/users
/posts
/comments
/orders
/products
...
```

Managing many endpoints can become complex.

---

# Disadvantages of GraphQL

GraphQL introduces its own challenges.

---

## More Complexity

Building GraphQL servers often requires:

* Schemas
* Resolvers
* Query management

This can increase development effort.

---

## Caching Is Harder

GraphQL typically uses a single endpoint.

Example:

```text id="graphql-endpoint"
/graphql
```

Caching strategies are often more complex than REST.

---

## Expensive Queries

Poorly designed queries can create performance issues.

Example:

```text id="deep-query"
User
↓
Posts
↓
Comments
↓
Replies
↓
More Data
```

Deep nesting can become expensive.

---

## Learning Curve

GraphQL introduces concepts many developers haven't encountered before.

---

## REST vs GraphQL Comparison Table

| Feature        | REST           | GraphQL           |
| -------------- | -------------- | ----------------- |
| Data Fetching  | Fixed Response | Client Controlled |
| Endpoints      | Multiple       | Usually One       |
| Caching        | Easy           | More Complex      |
| Learning Curve | Lower          | Higher            |
| Flexibility    | Moderate       | High              |
| Tooling        | Mature         | Strong            |
| Over-Fetching  | Possible       | Reduced           |
| Under-Fetching | Possible       | Reduced           |

Neither approach is universally better.

---

## When Should You Use REST?

REST is often a great choice when:

* APIs are simple
* Teams want predictable patterns
* Caching is important
* Existing infrastructure uses REST

Many successful applications rely entirely on REST.

---

## When Should You Use GraphQL?

GraphQL often shines when:

* Frontend data requirements vary
* Mobile bandwidth matters
* Multiple clients consume the same API
* Complex relationships exist between data

Large applications often benefit from GraphQL's flexibility.

## Common Misconceptions

### GraphQL Replaces REST

Not necessarily.

Many organizations use both.

---

### GraphQL Is Always Faster

Performance depends on implementation.

Poor GraphQL can be slower than good REST.

---

### REST Is Outdated

REST remains one of the most widely used API architectures.

---

### GraphQL Eliminates All API Problems

It solves some problems while introducing new trade-offs.

---

## A Simple Mental Model

Think of REST like ordering a predefined meal:

```text id="meal"
You Get What Is Included
```

Think of GraphQL like ordering from a menu:

```text id="menu"
You Choose Exactly What You Want
```

Both approaches can work well.

---

## FAQ

### Is GraphQL better than REST?

Not universally. The best choice depends on project requirements, team experience, and application complexity.

### Does GraphQL replace REST APIs?

No. Many companies successfully use both technologies together.

### Why do developers like GraphQL?

It allows clients to request exactly the data they need and often reduces the number of API requests.

### Why is REST still popular?

REST is simple, mature, easy to cache, and widely supported.

### Which should beginners learn first?

Most developers benefit from learning REST first because it is simpler and remains extremely common.

---

## Final Thoughts

REST and GraphQL are both valuable tools for building APIs.

REST excels in simplicity, predictability, and mature tooling. GraphQL excels in flexibility, efficient data fetching, and developer experience.

The real question isn't which technology is better. It's which technology is better for your specific project.

Understanding the strengths and trade-offs of both approaches will help you make smarter architectural decisions and build APIs that serve your users effectively.
